title: In France, canal boats ride a tank of water down a hillside instead of using locks

cover.alt: A steep grassy hillside beside a calm canal, with a long concrete ramp running down it from a white building at the top to a gate at the water’s edge.

body: The **Saint-Louis-Arzviller inclined plane** on the Marne–Rhine Canal opened in 1969 to replace a flight of 17 locks that took boats a whole day to get through. Now a boat sails into a steel tank full of water, about 41.5 m long, and the tank rolls down or up a slope of about 41% on a carriage, covering a height of 44.55 m. Two concrete counterweights of 450 tonnes each balance it, so its winches need relatively little power. Each run takes about four minutes and uses about 10 kWh of electricity.

slides.alt: Seen across a canal, a long steel tank on a carriage glides from the top of a steep concrete ramp all the way down to the gate at the water’s edge, while the camera slowly pans.
slides.caption: The water-filled tank of the Arzviller inclined plane rolls down the hillside to the lower canal. Sped up 8×: the real trip takes about four minutes.
slides.credit: Raimond Spekking · CC BY-SA 4.0 · excerpt, sped up 8×

slides.question: The 17 locks took a whole day. How many minutes does the inclined plane take, from going in to coming out?
slides.explanation: About 20 minutes in all, of which the slide itself takes about four.

slides.heading: A boat adds no weight
slides.text: A floating boat pushes out exactly its own weight of water, so the tank weighs the same whether a boat is sailing in, sailing out or not there at all. With its 730 m³ of water, the whole thing weighs about 900 tonnes, matched by the two counterweights, so the engines mainly control the speed.

slides.heading: Boats through Arzviller each year
slides.note: Pleasure boating peaked at 7,486 boats in 1999; about 150,000 visitors come to watch each year

slides.question: What does most of the work of lifting the 900-tonne tank?
slides.explanation: Two concrete counterweights of 450 tonnes each run on their own guided carriages, so the two electric winches need relatively little power.
